processing: A clonal tea plant cultivar rather than a finished tea, suited to high-grade green tea and to black tea. Hunan researchers have also made oolong, yellow and dark tea from it.
harvest_season: An early cultivar: spring one-bud-one-leaf shoots appear around early April.
appearance_dry: As green tea, deep and fresh green, in keeping with its high chlorophyll; shape depends on the maker.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green as a green tea, typical of the class.
appearance_wet: Tender green, as is typical of early spring shoots.
taste_profile: Floral-leaning in the greens made from it, and a study of oolong made from its summer leaf noted a floral aroma with a mellow taste.

brewing.notes: Green tea handling applies when it is sold as green; follow the normal rules for its class if it has been made into another type.

vintage_note: Rarely sold under its own name. Made as green tea it follows the usual pattern of the current year's harvest, with early spring lots most valued. Any other style made from it is sold according to that class.
description:
Bixiang Zao is an early, clonal, medium-leaf shrub cultivar linked with Hunan, valued for making high-grade green tea and black tea from the same plant. The name means roughly 'jade fragrance, early', which is a fair summary of why growers plant it.

It stands out in the lab as well as the garden. A study of varieties introduced to southern Henan found its chlorophyll and carotenoid levels well above the others tested, and judged it good for green tea, which fits with a deep green leaf.

It is unusually flexible. Hunan work has used it for floral-style green tea, for dark and yellow teas, and for an oolong from summer leaf with a floral aroma and mellow taste. That is research rather than market reality, but it shows how much the method can change the same leaf.

You will rarely see it on a label. If you do, ask how the tea was made and when it was picked, since the name of the plant tells you little about the tea in the packet.
history: Little is documented about who bred Bixiang Zao or when. What is clear is its modern life as a research and planting variety, with trials outside Hunan and processing studies published in the last few years.
